ta-l1d1q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus opening Thomas's commentary on the body of the Sentences. Having finished the prologue, Thomas characterizes Lombard's whole work as teaching divine things by seeking truth and refuting error, proceeding argumentatively and above all from authorities. Since everything theology considers falls under it insofar as it is referred to God as source and end, Lombard divides his subject matter by 'absolute' and 'related': first, with respect to cognition, into things (res) and signs; then, with respect to desire, into things to be enjoyed (fruibilia, desired for their own sake) and things to be used (utibilia, referred to another). Thomas maps the sub-parts of Distinction 1 accordingly, down to the reconciliation of Augustine's two accounts of use and enjoyment and the doubts about whether humans, God, and the virtues are users, enjoyers, or objects of use and enjoyment. He then announces a threefold inquiry (on uti and frui; on what is usable and enjoyable; on those who use and enjoy), the first of which asks what enjoyment and use are in reality.
claims: Everything treated in theology falls under its consideration insofar as it is referred to God as its source and end.
Lombard divides his subject matter by absolute and related, first with respect to cognition (things and signs) and then with respect to desire (things to be enjoyed and things to be used).

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3578.summary: First objection, arguing that enjoyment is an act of the intellect. The noblest act belongs to the noblest power; the intellect is the highest human power; and enjoyment, since it places a human in their ultimate end, is the most perfect human act. So enjoyment belongs to the intellect.
claims: The most perfect act belongs to the highest power, and the intellect is the highest power in a human being.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3581.summary: Second argument for the intellect. Augustine says that vision is the whole reward, and the reward of all merit consists in enjoying the divinity. So enjoyment is essentially vision, which is an act of the intellect.
claims: If vision is the whole reward and the reward is enjoyment, then enjoyment is essentially vision.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3584.summary: A contrary argument that enjoyment is an act of the will. An act is specified by its object; the object of enjoyment is the enjoyable thing, the ultimate end; and the end, having the character of good, is the object of the will.
claims: Acts are specified by their objects.
The ultimate end, as good, is the object of the will.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3588.summary: Second argument for the will, from Augustine's definition: we enjoy things known in which the will, delighted, rests for their own sake. Since the will appears in the definition, enjoyment seems to be the will's act rather than the intellect's.
claims: Augustine defines enjoyment through the will's delighted rest in what is known.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3594.summary: A third line of argument, that enjoyment belongs to all the powers. Reward corresponds to merit; a human merits through all their powers and so will be rewarded through all of them; and the reward is enjoyment itself.
claims: Reward corresponds to merit, and merit is gained through all the powers.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3597.summary: Supporting argument for enjoyment in all powers. Augustine says that a human will find pasture within, in the Saviour's divinity, and without, in his humanity. So the exterior powers as well as the interior ones will enjoy.
claims: The blessed will find delight both in Christ's divinity (inwardly) and in his humanity (outwardly).

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3600.summary: A fourth position, that enjoyment belongs to no power. Every act is named from the power whose act it is, as understanding is named from the intellect, but 'enjoying' is named from no power.
claims: Every act is denominated from the power to which it belongs.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3603.summary: Turning to which habit enjoyment is the act of, the argument holds that it belongs to charity alone. Charity is the perfect virtue (1 Cor. 13), and according to the Philosopher happiness is the operation of perfect virtue. So enjoyment, in which all our happiness consists, is the act of charity.
claims: Happiness is the operation of perfect virtue, and charity is the perfect virtue.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3606.summary: Confirms the previous argument from Augustine's definition cited in Lombard's text: to enjoy is to cling by love to a thing for its own sake. Since love is the act of charity, enjoyment belongs to charity.
claims: Enjoyment is defined as clinging by love to something for its own sake.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3616.summary: Argues that enjoyment is not the act of charity alone. Three things come together in enjoyment: perfect vision, full comprehension, and the clinging of consummated love. So it seems to be the act also of what succeeds faith and hope.
claims: Enjoyment involves perfect vision, full comprehension, and consummated love, which succeed faith, hope, and charity.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3619.summary: Further argument that enjoyment belongs to every virtue. Enjoyment joins us to God, and every virtue joins us to God, since virtue is the disposition of the perfect to the best (Physics 7).
claims: Every virtue, as the disposition of the perfect to the best, joins us to God.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3622.summary: Thomas's determination. Enjoyment is ultimate human happiness and so lies in the best operation, not in a habit: the operation of the highest power (the intellect) on the noblest object (God). Vision of the divine essence is therefore the whole substance of beatitude. Because God is seen through his essence and not through a likeness, what is seen comes to be within the seer; this is comprehension, which succeeds hope as vision succeeds faith. What is thus received unites the seer to itself by love in a kind of mutual penetration, and the highest delight follows on union with what is most fitting. 'Enjoyment' names this happiness from the side of its completion, since it includes delight, rather than from its principle. So enjoyment is an act of the will under the habit of charity, though in an ordering to the preceding powers and habits.
claims: Happiness consists in operation, not in a habit.
The vision of God through his essence is the whole substance of beatitude.
Enjoyment names beatitude from the side of its completion in delight and is therefore an act of the will under charity, presupposing intellectual vision.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3641.summary: Reply to the first objection. Appetite always follows cognition, so the higher part of the soul, like the lower, has a cognitive and an appetitive power. The intellect is higher in origin, the will in perfection, and the same order holds for their habits and their acts of vision and love. Enjoyment names the highest operation with respect to its perfection.
claims: The intellect is prior in origin, but the will is higher in respect of perfection.
Enjoyment names the highest operation with respect to its perfection.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3644.summary: Reply to the second objection. Vision has the full character of happiness only as an operation perfected by what follows it, since delight perfects an operation as beauty perfects youth (Ethics 10).
claims: Vision has the full character of happiness only as perfected by the delight that follows it.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3651.summary: Concedes the two arguments for the will.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3655.summary: Reply to the arguments that all powers enjoy. Enjoyment in the proper sense cannot belong to the lower powers. Being material powers, they have no operation concerning the ultimate end, which they do not apprehend. But just as the intellect now gains perfection by receiving from the lower powers, in heaven the reverse will hold, and the perfection and joy of the higher part will overflow into the lower. This is how Augustine's statement that sense will be turned into reason is to be understood.
claims: Material powers cannot properly enjoy, since they do not apprehend the ultimate end.
In glory, the joy of the higher part overflows into the lower powers.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3664.summary: Reply to the argument from pasture in Christ's humanity. The humanity of Christ is not the ultimate end. So seeing it will not be enjoyment in the proper sense but an accidental joy, not substantial beatitude.
claims: Christ's humanity is not the ultimate end, so the vision of it is accidental joy, not substantial beatitude.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3667.summary: Reply to the argument that enjoyment belongs to no power. An act that belongs absolutely to one power is named from it, but an act of one power in an ordering to another is named from neither. Scientific knowing, for example, is an act of reason ordered to intellect, as deriving conclusions from principles. Likewise enjoying is an act of the will that follows on the intellect's act, the open vision of God.
claims: An act of one power in an ordering to another is denominated from neither power.
Enjoyment is an act of the will consequent on the intellect's open vision of God.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3670.summary: Concedes the two arguments that enjoyment belongs to charity.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3673.summary: Reply to the argument from the three concurrent elements. Although vision, comprehension, and love come together in enjoyment, it is perfected in love, as the body of the article showed.
claims: Enjoyment, though involving vision and comprehension, is perfected in love.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3676.summary: Reply to the last argument. The other virtues join us to God by way of merit and disposition, but only charity does so by way of perfect union.
claims: Only charity joins us to God by way of perfect union; the other virtues do so by way of merit and disposition.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3688.summary: First argument that use is an act of reason. Ordering one thing to another belongs to a comparing power, which reason is, and use implies ordering to an end.
claims: Ordering one thing to another belongs to reason.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3691.summary: Second argument for reason. According to the Philosopher, ordering the means to an end belongs to prudence, a habit of reason. So use, which implies such ordering, is an act of reason.
claims: Ordering means to an end belongs to prudence, a habit of reason.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3694.summary: A contrary argument that use is an act of the will, since the will appears in its definition: to use is to take something into the faculty of the will.
claims: Augustine defines use as taking something into the faculty of the will.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3698.summary: Second argument for the will. What is ordered to an end belongs to the same power that attains the end, and enjoyment, the attainment of the end, has been shown to be an act of the will. So use is too.
claims: Use, as ordered to the end, belongs to the same power as enjoyment, which attains the end.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3701.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Use' is said in several ways. It can mean any operation, as in Augustine's definition (taking something into the faculty of the will, i.e. operating with it at the will's command), or frequency of operation, i.e. custom, as in Victorinus. In both these senses use can be the act of any power. In the sense relevant here, use concerns what is ordered to an end. Something is brought to its end by three operations: reason fixing and directing it to the end, the will commanding, and the motive power executing. Use names the execution of what has been ordered to the end, taken generally rather than as the proper act of a particular motive power. So it is an act of the will, the universal mover of the powers, in an ordering to reason.
claims: 'Use' has several senses: any operation, habitual operation, and the employment of means to an end.
A means is brought to its end by reason's direction, the will's command, and the motive power's execution.
Use in the proper sense is an act of the will as universal mover of the powers, presupposing reason's ordering.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3716.summary: Reply to the first objection. Use presupposes an ordering by reason, but its substance lies rather in the will's execution.
claims: Use presupposes rational ordering, but its substance lies in the will's execution.

ta-l1d1q1-d1e3719.summary: Reply to the second objection. Prudence perfects practical reason as right, and the rightness or truth of practical reason consists in conformity with right appetite (Ethics 6). So prudence perfects not only acts of reason but also acts of will regulated by reason; choice, for example, is an act of the will or free decision but still belongs to prudence.
claims: The truth of practical reason consists in conformity with right appetite.
Prudence extends to acts of will regulated by reason, such as choice.

ta-l1d1q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium to Book I, Distinction 1 places Lombard's division of theology's subject matter into things and signs, and into what is to be enjoyed and what is to be used, within the order of the whole work. Theology considers everything as referred to God. The Prooemium also sets out the threefold inquiry that follows, beginning with what enjoyment and use are.

ta-l1d1q1-Dd1e3570.summary: Article 1 asks to which power and habit enjoyment (frui) belongs. Objections assign it to the intellect (the highest power; vision as the whole reward), to the will (its object is the good; Augustine's definition), to all the powers (reward follows merit), or to none (it takes its name from no power). A second set asks whether it belongs to charity alone or to all the virtues. Thomas answers that beatitude consists in the best operation, the intellect's vision of God through his essence. From this vision follow comprehension and a loving union, and from union the highest delight. 'Enjoyment' names beatitude from the side of this delightful completion, so it is an act of the will under charity, presupposing the intellect's vision. The replies distinguish the intellect's priority in origin from the will's priority in perfection. They explain that the lower powers share in joy only by overflow, treat the vision of Christ's humanity as accidental joy, account for acts named from no power, and hold that charity alone unites us to God by perfect union.
claims: Enjoyment is an act of the will under the habit of charity, consequent on and ordered to the intellect's vision of God.
The vision of God through his essence is the substance of beatitude, completed by delight.

ta-l1d1q1-Dd1e3680.summary: Article 2 asks whether use (uti) is an act of reason or of the will. Arguments for reason appeal to the rational character of ordering means to ends and to prudence; arguments for the will appeal to Augustine's definition and to the parallel with enjoyment. Thomas distinguishes senses of 'use' and analyses how means are brought to their end: by reason's direction, the will's command, and the motive power's execution. Use properly names the execution of what has been ordered to the end, so it is an act of the will as universal mover, presupposing reason's ordering. Prudence extends to such acts because practical truth is conformity with right appetite.
claims: Use in the proper sense is an act of the will executing what reason has ordered to an end.
Prudence perfects acts of will regulated by reason.

ta-l1d1q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 1 asks what enjoyment and use are in reality, the first of three inquiries arising from Lombard's Augustinian division of things into what is to be enjoyed and what is to be used. After a Prooemium mapping Lombard's text, Article 1 locates enjoyment in the will under charity. It is the delight that completes the intellect's vision of the divine essence, which is itself the substance of beatitude. Article 2 locates use in the will too, as the executive employment of means that reason has ordered to an end. Taken together, the articles set out an account of the soul's ordering to God: the intellect supplies vision and order, while the will, by enjoying the end and using the means, completes and executes that ordering.
claims: Enjoyment is an act of the will under charity, completing the intellect's vision of God through delight.
Use is an act of the will executing what reason has ordered to the end.
Intellect is prior in origin, but the will completes the ordering to the end.
